target.title: LipLearner: Customizable Silent Speech Interactions on Mobile Devices
target.venue: Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '23)

entries.text: The authors propose a contrastively pretrained lipreading encoder with few-shot, in-situ customization for new silent-speech commands.
entries.condition: Encoder is pretrained on public visual speech data; the user-specific linear classifier is trained from a few examples.
entries.quote: We propose a few-shot lipreading framework that enables in-situ silent speech command customization.

entries.text: Novel commands can be arbitrary phrases, languages, or non-verbal lip gestures, with at least one sample.
entries.condition: Author-stated capability of few-shot customization; the evaluation covers a particular collected command set and a 16-person user study.
entries.quote: Hence, the user can freely define any phrase in any language, or even non-verbal lip gestures, as a silent speech command by providing at least one sample.

entries.text: The encoder is frozen during user customization; only the linear classifier is fine-tuned, enabling on-device adaptation.
entries.condition: User-dependent classifier trained on each user's data; recognition and fine-tuning run on the phone.
entries.quote: In the fine-tuning stage, we freeze the weights of the encoder model and only train the linear classifier, thus making it trivial to perform in-situ command customization on mobile devices.

entries.text: The authors present visual keyword spotting as a new activation method for lipreading interfaces, using the encoder's embeddings and user-defined keyword samples.
entries.condition: Few-shot keyword enrollment; similarity threshold plus a binary classifier rechecks suspected activations.
entries.quote: Although KWS as an activation method has been predominant in voice interactions, to our best knowledge, this technique has not yet been applied in lipreading-based interfaces.

entries.text: The authors claim superiority over a conventional user-dependent train-from-scratch approach despite using fewer enrollment samples.
entries.condition: Introductory comparison says the conventional approach used four times more training data; Sec. 5.4 compares a 6-shot model with 30 samples per command.

entries.text: Online incremental learning is intended to extend the command vocabulary and improve recognition as new samples arrive.
entries.condition: Active learning solicits user confirmation/correction when training data are sparse; on-demand mode adds only corrected errors.

entries.text: Voice2Lip reduces enrollment effort by pairing a spoken utterance with its speech-recognizer text label.
entries.condition: One-shot command registration; user may edit the recognized text or type a label instead.
entries.quote: To register a new command, the user just says it aloud, and then our system will learn the lip movements using the text recognized from voice signals as labels.

entries.text: The prototype performs recognition and fine-tuning locally, without a network connection, to address privacy concerns.
entries.condition: iOS prototype evaluated on iPhone 13 Pro; data stored locally.
entries.quote: Thus, LipLearner can be used without network connections and has all data stored locally, addressing the privacy concerns in lipreading.

entries.text: The authors report that the user study supports usability and learnability of customizable silent-speech interaction.
entries.condition: Subjective feedback from 16 participants; SUS questionnaire and semi-structured interviews.

entries.text: Contrastive pretraining uses LRW: 500 word classes with up to 1,000 utterances per word; the model starts from Feng et al.'s pretrained weights.
entries.condition: Public BBC-news LRW video segments; hundreds of speakers; 29 frames at 25 fps in the paper's description.

entries.text: Paper reports initial learning rate 3×10^-4, a factor-0.5 ReduceLROnPlateau schedule after 40 stagnant validation-loss epochs, and 500-epoch convergence.
entries.unit: learning rate; scheduler factor; epochs before reduction; epochs to convergence
entries.condition: Contrastive LRW pretraining; best-loss checkpoint selected on validation set.

entries.text: Reported contrastive pretraining duration and hardware.
entries.unit: epochs; hours (across 2 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti GPUs)
entries.condition: LRW contrastive pretraining; loss convergence and time reported by the authors.

entries.text: The in-the-wild test corpus contains 25 assistant-command sentences spanning 3–22 visemes, with mean length 10.08 ± 4.47 visemes.
entries.condition: Command prompts adapted from Alexa-command research and Apple's Siri guide; spoken by 11 local-university speakers.

entries.text: In-the-wild data collection comprised 11 speakers, 7 sessions, 25 commands, and 5 repetitions per command.
entries.condition: 11 speakers (4 female, 7 male; all right-handed) × 7 condition sessions × 25 commands × 5 repetitions; iPhone 11/iPhone 13 Pro, 1080×1920 at 30 fps.

entries.text: Seven collection conditions span outdoor daylight, low/artificial light, seated/standing/walking posture, and right/left/both-hand grasp conditions.
entries.condition: Cross-factor combinations identified as C1–C7; collection condition, not a single full factorial of all factor levels.
entries.quote: All participants completed seven collection sessions, each of which is under a condition that is a combination of the three key factors (see Figure 4).

entries.text: Customization freezes the visual encoder and trains a user-dependent logistic-regression classifier on that user's feature vectors.
entries.condition: Classifier trained per user; the paper does not give logistic-regression regularization or feature-scaling settings.
entries.quote: Note that the linear classifier is user-dependent and trained on each user’s data to maximize accuracy.

entries.text: Five-command test: one-shot and three-shot mean F1 scores.
entries.condition: Experiment 1; 5 commands; last 2 samples in all conditions held out; N training shots sampled from remaining data across conditions; 1,000 repeated selections; 11 speakers.

entries.text: Twenty-five-command test: one-shot and four-shot mean F1 scores.
entries.condition: Experiment 1; 25 commands; 11 speakers; last 2 samples in all conditions held out; shots randomly selected from remaining conditions; 1,000 repeated selections.
entries.quote: the model still obtains a one-shot F1-score of 0.8947 ± 0.0530 when classifying 25 commands and an F1-score of 0.9819 ± 0.0120 was achieved with four shots.

entries.text: Experiment 1 reports 1,000 random repetitions but does not report the seed values, RNG implementation, or whether the same sampled selections are reused across conditions.
entries.condition: Five- through 25-command F1 experiments; repetition count is stated, individual seeds and selection schedule are not.
entries.quote: Since there are too many possible combinations of data selection, we repeated the test 1000 times to simulate that training data is collected over various conditions in daily use.

entries.text: The paper does not report an explicit chance-level or simple baseline for the 5–25-command F1 experiments.
entries.condition: Experiment 1 classification results in Fig. 6; chance level is not stated or calculated in the paper.
entries.quote: The model’s performance improved rapidly as the number of shots increased.

entries.text: The paper does not specify the F1 averaging convention or the exact aggregation unit underlying the reported mean ± SD in Experiment 1.
entries.condition: F1 for 5–25 command classifications; participant-, command-, and repetition-level aggregation is not fully defined.
entries.quote: The standard deviation was also reduced when the number of shots was increased, indicating that more training samples can improve the model’s robustness.

entries.condition: Table 2 and Sec. 5.5; per-speaker/command aggregation and chance baseline are not supplied.
entries.quote: Overall, we conclude our framework still shows high and robust performance even in unseen conditions, which is promising for real-world applications.

entries.text: The paper does not report whether LRW pretraining speakers overlap with the 11 model-test speakers or the 16 user-study participants.
entries.condition: Speaker identities and cross-dataset speaker-disjointness are not given for the test cohorts.

entries.text: The exact train/validation partitioning and validation-set selection protocol for choosing the pretrained encoder are not described in the paper.
entries.condition: The text states that the checkpoint with least validation loss is saved, but does not specify split creation or validation data selection.

entries.text: Pixel-value scaling, classifier feature normalization, and logistic-regression regularization are not reported for the command-classification evaluations.
entries.condition: Paper reports grayscale resizing and normalized embeddings for cosine KWS, but not scaling/regularization for the user-dependent logistic-regression evaluation.

entries.text: The leave-one-condition-out descriptions do not state whether the same 11 speakers contribute both enrollment and test samples, although results are summarized across those speakers.
entries.condition: Within-speaker personalization is described, but speaker-level partitioning or an unseen-speaker test is not reported for these evaluations.

entries.text: For continuous keyword spotting, the system uses a 0.6 similarity trigger, a 0.65 end-of-speech similarity threshold, a 30-frame window, a 1.5-second delay before end detection, and a 4-second maximum utterance.
entries.unit: similarity; similarity; frames (about 1 s); seconds; seconds maximum utterance
entries.condition: An additional binary classifier rechecks suspected keyword positives; EOS uses similarity to the non-speaking sample without an additional classifier.

entries.text: The on-device prototype reports approximately 422 ms total processing latency for 30-frame feature extraction and classification.
entries.condition: iPhone 13 Pro iOS prototype; 30-frame input; feature extraction 250 ms and classification 172 ms.
entries.quote: The system latency was approximately 250ms feature extraction for 30 frames + 172ms classification ≈422ms, which is sufficient for real-time interactions.

entries.text: On-device incremental model update time with the stated command/sample configuration.
entries.condition: iPhone 13 Pro; 30 commands × 5 shots = 150 training samples; classifier-only on-device update.
entries.quote: 2217ms (10-test average) with 30 commands × 5 shots = 150 samples as training data

entries.text: Active learning asks the user to confirm a prediction; an incorrect prediction is corrected by selecting the correct label from existing commands.
entries.condition: Paper says this mode is used when training data are sparse (e.g., fewer than 3 shots).

entries.text: On-demand learning collects no data proactively; users add only samples that they correct after recognition.
entries.condition: User-selected correction mode after the user considers the model sufficiently accurate.

entries.text: The user study enrolled 16 voice-assistant-experienced participants and used 30 commands: 10 fixed English, 10 scenario-described, and 10 freely created.
entries.condition: iPhone 13 Pro; multilingual participants; one-shot Voice2Lip enrollment; live recognition test comprised six trials, each issuing all 30 commands once.

entries.text: One-shot model trained from voice enrollment: accuracy for vocalized and silent test utterances.
entries.unit: % accuracy (mean ± SD), voiced; % accuracy (mean ± SD), silent
entries.condition: 16-person live study; 30 commands; first two trials; model enrolled from voice input; order of voice/silent trials counterbalanced; only silent-trial sample retained for incremental learning.
entries.quote: first, we find that the one-shot model whose training data all comes from voice input had better accuracy in recognizing vocalized utterances (87.29%±10.42%) than recognizing unvocalized utterances (81.67%±12.80%).

entries.text: Live user-study recognition accuracy after incremental learning at 3 and 5 shots.
entries.unit: % accuracy (mean ± SD), 3 shots; % accuracy (mean ± SD), 5 shots

entries.quote: The accuracy rose from 96.04%±4.12% with 3 shots to 98.75%± 2.60% with 5 shots.

entries.text: Number of participants reaching perfect accuracy by five-shot enrollment.

entries.text: The user-study accuracy results do not specify whether mean ± SD is aggregated over participants, trials, or command instances; no chance-level baseline is reported.

entries.text: Preliminary profile-face wearable test accuracies.

entries.text: Authors concede active learning still imposes physical and cognitive effort; they suggest speech-based confirmation/correction rather than button tapping.
entries.condition: Limitation of the current interaction design; future work should improve user involvement in the learning loop.

entries.text: Authors concede tolerance to phrasing variation may make similar commands difficult to distinguish; “Turn on the light” and “Turn on the flashlight” are a common confusion.
entries.condition: They propose more samples for low-accuracy commands or asking users to rephrase.

entries.text: Authors concede command abstraction remains limited without context: separate commands are needed for different alarm times.
entries.condition: They propose future zero-shot lipreading jointly trained with language models such as GPT-3 or T5.

entries.text: Authors say selecting the best keyword similarity threshold for all users is impossible and recommend exposing the setting to user choice in future work.
entries.condition: User-study KWS used a fixed similarity threshold; false-negative reduction may increase false positives.
entries.quote: However, since determining the best threshold for all users is impossible, future work should open this setting to the user’s choice.

entries.text: Prior few-shot wrist-gesture customization result cited as a comparison: 1-shot accuracy was 55.3% for 12 gestures.
entries.condition: Prior study [68], smartwatch IMU gesture recognition; paper notes its supervised pretraining and laptop data augmentation.

entries.text: The public training script uses batch size 500 and one visible GPU; the paper does not state the batch size, and describes training across two RTX 2080 Ti GPUs.
entries.condition: Repository train.sh arguments; training script's effective learning rate is batch-size/GPU-scaled.

entries.text: The public pretraining code scales decoded grayscale pixel values by 1/255; this pixel normalization is not stated in the paper's preprocessing description.
entries.condition: Applied to decoded LRW frames before augmentation; training and validation then use different spatial crops.

entries.text: The code expects class/phase folders and samples paired examples from each of 500 classes; train and validation phases are loaded separately.
entries.condition: Per-class files are shuffled, two examples are popped per class to form paired batches, and collection stops when any class has fewer than two left.

entries.text: Training code uses random distortion/frame dropping/cropping, 0.5-probability horizontal flip, and color jitter; validation uses a deterministic center crop to 88×88.
entries.condition: pretraining/utils/dataset.py and cvtransforms.py; the paper names augmentation types but omits these implementation settings.

entries.text: The checked-in pretraining scripts do not set explicit Python, NumPy, or Torch random seeds; the paper does not provide pretraining seed values.
entries.condition: Applies to the available LRW pretraining entry point; the repository contains no scripts reproducing the paper's experiment 1/2 evaluation repetitions.

entries.text: Repository README says the app works best on iPhone 11 or newer; for older phones it recommends disabling KWS if inference exceeds the sliding-window duration.
entries.condition: Deployment guidance from README; the paper's application evaluation used iPhone 13 Pro.

entries.text: The repository README describes an added silent-speech activity detector that gates keyword detection on an open mouth and explicitly says this was not used in the paper's user study.
entries.condition: Repository implementation note; distinguish the later app code from the reported study protocol.

questions.q: What protocol supports the paper's strongest unseen-condition superiority claim?
questions.answer: The leave-one-condition-out test holds out one of seven recorded conditions, trains the few-shot model using one sample per class from each of the other six conditions, and compares it with a supervised counterpart trained on 30 samples per command. The reported F1 averages are 0.9895 ± 0.0078 versus 0.7147 ± 0.2576; this is condition generalization within the collected speaker cohort, not a reported speaker-disjoint test.

questions.q: How does the 30-command result change with user enrollment, and what is the live-study protocol?
questions.answer: In the 16-person live study, one-shot accuracy was 81.67 ± 12.80% on silent utterances; accuracy rose to 96.04 ± 4.12% at three shots and 98.75 ± 2.60% at five shots. Participants issued 30 commands once in each of six trials and added samples through active learning. The paper does not define the mean/SD aggregation unit or report a chance baseline.

questions.q: What evaluation details limit reproduction or interpretation of the reported metrics?
questions.answer: The paper omits fixed seeds, exact LRW validation-partition selection, some cross-condition shot-allocation details, feature scaling and logistic-regression settings, speaker-overlap analysis, metric aggregation conventions, and explicit chance baselines. The available repository exposes pretraining code rather than experiment-evaluation scripts; its data loader adds pixel scaling and concrete augmentation/sampling behavior.

questions.q: What limitations do the authors themselves acknowledge?
questions.answer: Active learning still requires physical/cognitive effort; tolerance to phrasing variation can confuse similar commands; commands lack contextual abstraction; and a single fixed KWS threshold cannot be optimal for all users.

questions.q: How are contrastive positives and negatives formed on LRW, and is pretraining called self-supervised?
questions.answer: Pairs are formed by LRW word class: each group contains a sample from each class, and the second group supplies another sample from those same classes, so positives are same-word utterances and negatives are different-word utterances—not two augmentations of a single clip. The paper calls the approach semi-supervised (and describes its supervision as weak), not self-supervised.

questions.q: Which pretrained weights start the encoder, and is contrastive pretraining ablated against them?
questions.answer: The encoder starts from pre-trained weights provided by Feng et al.; the paper describes that architecture as a lipreading-classification model and defines conventional supervised learning as classifying labeled inputs into known classes, but does not explicitly state the objective used to train Feng's checkpoint. It reports no few-shot ablation against the original Feng encoder or cross-entropy features; its Sec. 5.4 comparator is a separate supervised model trained from scratch.

questions.q: What exactly is the Sec. 5.4 counterpart?
questions.answer: The counterpart is the authors' own implementation: it has the encoder's architecture, is supervised and user-dependent/train-from-scratch, and uses that user's data from the six training conditions (30 samples per command). The results are summarized across the 11 model-test participants; the paper does not identify a particular published system as the counterpart.

questions.q: Which activation methods does the paper name as prior, and does it cite or compare visual keyword spotting?
questions.answer: The paper describes mouth-opening-degree detection, offline segmentation, and trigger buttons; it also mentions gaze-based selection as a multimodal interaction, not as a lipreading wake-up method. It says visual KWS had not previously been applied in lipreading interfaces to the authors' knowledge; it does not compare with visual-KWS systems, although some lipreading/audio-visual papers by the example authors appear in other contexts.

questions.q: How many enrollment samples, which similarity and which negatives underlie the 6.75% EER?
questions.answer: Sec. 6.1 does not specify the number of enrollment samples per keyword used for the EER analysis; its general method description refers to comparison with a keyword utterance sample. Similarity is cosine similarity between normalized vectors, and the negative set is utterances of all other commands. The reported average EER is 6.75%.

questions.q: How is the voiced-enrolled one-shot model scored on voiced vs silent utterances, and is silent enrollment compared?
questions.answer: The first two trials test the same command set, one command per trial, with one trial voiced and one silent; trial order is counterbalanced. Voice2Lip's voice-enrolled one-shot model scores 87.29% on voiced versus 81.67% on silent utterances, and the paper discusses this gap, but it does not report a separate one-shot accuracy comparison using silent-sample enrollment; silent-trial data is used only for the second-shot update.

questions.q: Are user-study test utterances added to training for later trials?
questions.answer: Yes, the protocol collects each recognized or corrected utterance as a sample and obtains one new sample per command at trial end. Participants could then update the model, so later trials could be scored using earlier same-participant test utterances if they performed the update; for the first two trials, only silent-trial samples were allowed as the second shot.

questions.q: Does the paper cite prior few-shot or one-shot lipreading personalization?
questions.answer: For few-shot learning, the paper cites work on sound recognition and human activity recognition, and identifies few-shot gesture recognition using smartwatch IMU signals as the most relevant literature. It does not cite prior few-shot/one-shot lipreading personalization or few-shot silent-speech enrollment with another sensor in Secs. 2.2–2.3 or the references.

questions.q: Are the 11 test speakers or the command words in LRW?
questions.answer: The paper reports an LRW pretraining vocabulary of 500 word classes, a 25-sentence model-test command corpus, and 11 recruited model-test speakers. It does not report whether those speakers appeared in LRW or whether any words in the command phrases overlap with LRW's vocabulary, so actual speaker or word overlap is unstated.
